venues.name: Bvlgari Hotel Shanghai
venues.note: The Roman maison's 48-storey jewel, set inside the restored 1920s Shanghai Chamber of Commerce, glamour with a Bulgari signature.

venues.name: The Peninsula Shanghai
venues.note: The last great building raised on the Bund, an Art Deco grande dame with celadon walls and the river at its feet.

venues.name: Capella Shanghai, Jian Ye Li
venues.note: Fifty-five restored shikumen lane houses turned into private villas, the most secluded luxury in the city.

venues.name: Amanyangyun
venues.note: An Aman built from a transplanted Ming forest and camphor-wood mansions, a serene estate an hour from the towers.

venues.name: Mandarin Oriental Pudong, Shanghai
venues.note: The group's riverside flagship, a calm, contemporary house looking straight across the Huangpu to the Bund.

venues.name: The Ritz-Carlton Shanghai, Pudong
venues.note: A modern Art Deco tower high in Lujiazui, with the legendary Flair rooftop and full-frontal Bund views.

venues.name: Waldorf Astoria Shanghai on the Bund
venues.note: The old Shanghai Club reborn, home of the Long Bar, all dark wood and colonial-era grandeur on the southern Bund.

venues.name: The Middle House
venues.note: Piero Lissoni's serene, design-led house from the Swire stable, the quietest luxury in central Shanghai.

venues.name: The PuLi Hotel and Spa
venues.note: An urban-resort sanctuary beside Jing'an Park, a long infinity pool, a great spa, and a genuinely tranquil city retreat.

venues.name: InterContinental Shanghai Wonderland
venues.note: The 'deep pit' hotel built into a flooded quarry cliff, 18 storeys, two of them underwater, and unlike anywhere else on earth.

venues.name: Ultraviolet by Paul Pairet
venues.note: A single table for ten, a secret address, and a psycho-taste tour of sound, scent and vision, the most theatrical meal in Asia.

venues.name: Taian Table
venues.note: Chef Stefan Stiller's precise, produce-led modern European tasting menu at an open counter, three stars, quietly held.

venues.name: 8½ Otto e Mezzo BOMBANA
venues.note: Umberto Bombana's grand Italian on the Bund, white truffle in season and a room built for occasions.

venues.name: Da Vittorio Shanghai
venues.note: The Cerea family's Bergamo institution, transplanted to Shanghai, the paccheri Vittorio is worth the crossing.

venues.name: Fu He Hui
venues.note: Tony Lu's zen temple to Chinese vegetarian fine dining, meat-free courses of real depth across three hushed floors.

venues.name: Canton 8 (Huangpu)
venues.note: Chef Chan Yan Tak's protégé kitchen, pristine, classical Cantonese that has held two stars for years.

venues.name: Imperial Treasure Fine Chinese Cuisine
venues.note: Grand, classical Cantonese and Peking duck in a polished Bund-front room, a benchmark banquet address.

venues.name: Ji Pin Court
venues.note: Refined, restrained Cantonese cooking in a serene setting, two stars earned on precision, not spectacle.

venues.name: Bao Li Xuan
venues.note: Elegant Cantonese inside the Bulgari, silk-lined rooms, creek views and cooking of real finesse.

venues.name: Meet the Bund
venues.note: Chef DeAille Tam's inventive Fujian-rooted cooking, named the best restaurant on the Chinese mainland.
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Restaurants 2025 (No. 14, Best Restaurant on the Chinese Mainland)

venues.name: Ling Long
venues.note: Chef Jason Liu's set menu chases xian (umami) on a course-by-course journey across regional China, inventive and personal.

venues.name: Il Ristorante – Niko Romito
venues.note: Niko Romito's essential, pared-back Italian inside the Bulgari, deceptively simple, deeply exact.

venues.name: Xin Rong Ji
venues.note: The celebrated Taizhou seafood house, pristine yellow croaker and coastal Zhejiang cooking at its finest.

venues.name: Fu 1088
venues.note: Refined Shanghainese in a 1930s garden villa of private rooms, old-money Shanghai dining, room by room.

venues.name: Yong Yi Ting
venues.note: Elegant Jiangnan cooking, the delicate, sweet-savoury flavours of the Yangtze delta, beautifully rendered.

venues.name: Maison Lameloise
venues.note: The Shanghai outpost of the storied three-star Burgundy house, classical French haute cuisine high over the river.

venues.name: Da Dong (Jing'an)
venues.note: The roast-duck maestro's Shanghai kitchen, lean, lacquered Peking duck and modern Chinese theatre.

venues.name: Yong Fu (Maoming Road)
venues.note: Genteel Ningbo cooking in a former French Concession mansion, seafood-led and quietly aristocratic.

venues.name: Canton Table
venues.note: Modern Cantonese and dim sum with a Bund view, an easy, polished lunch or relaxed dinner.

venues.name: Cheng Long Hang
venues.note: Homely, hearty Shanghainese done properly, red-braised pork and drunken crab in an unfussy neighbourhood room.

venues.name: The Bund (Waitan)
venues.note: The mile-long riverfront promenade where 1920s European stone facades face the neon towers of Pudong across the water. Walk it at dusk when the whole skyline switches on, then let your driver collect you for dinner up on the strip.

venues.name: Huangpu River Evening Cruise
venues.note: The Bund and the Pudong skyline are best seen from the middle of the river, both lit and mirrored on the water at once. A private charter with dinner aboard turns forty minutes of glow into the evening's centrepiece for the whole family.

venues.name: Shanghai Tower Observation Deck
venues.note: China's tallest building and one of the highest observatories on earth, reached by a lift that climbs 118 floors in under a minute. On a clear day the city unrolls in every direction; the twisting glass skin softens the wind far below.

venues.name: Shanghai World Financial Center Observatory
venues.note: The 'bottle opener' tower whose 100th-floor Sky Walk is a glass-floored bridge suspended 474 metres over the city. Children and grandparents alike freeze at the edge before daring the transparent floor.

venues.name: Oriental Pearl Tower
venues.note: The pink-sphered TV tower that became Shanghai's postcard symbol, with a glass-floor walkway ringing one of its orbs. Dated but beloved, it is the shot every first-time visitor wants of themselves against the skyline.

venues.name: Yu Garden (Yuyuan)
venues.note: A Ming-dynasty scholar's garden of rockeries, koi ponds, dragon-topped walls and moon gates, laid out over four centuries ago. A private guide reads the hidden symbolism in each pavilion so the labyrinth becomes a story rather than a crowd.

venues.name: Yuyuan Bazaar & City God Temple
venues.note: The warren of upturned-eave shophouses around the garden, thick with silk, jade, tea and steaming dumpling stalls beside the working Taoist City God Temple. Loud, festive and photogenic; go early with a guide before the tour buses land.

venues.name: Nanxiang Steamed Bun Restaurant (xiaolongbao)
venues.note: The century-old teahouse in the Yu Garden bazaar that made Shanghai's soup dumplings famous, still folding them by hand. Ask for a private upstairs table and vegetable-filled baskets so vegetarian travellers share in the ritual.

venues.name: Shanghai Museum (People's Square)
venues.note: The bronze-ding-shaped building holding one of the world's great collections of Chinese bronzes, ceramics, jade, painting and calligraphy. A calm, air-conditioned afternoon of five thousand years of craft, ideal with a scholar-guide.

venues.name: Shanghai Museum East
venues.note: The vast new Pudong wing, opened in full in 2024 and nearly double the original in size, with eight galleries devoted mostly to ancient Chinese art. The showpiece is the panoramic top-floor view back across the river to the People's Square building.

venues.name: Museum of Contemporary Art Shanghai (MoCA)
venues.note: A glass pavilion set in People's Park showing rotating international and Chinese contemporary shows, a cool counterpoint to the antiquities nearby. Small enough to fold into a morning without tiring younger travellers.

venues.name: West Bund Museum (Centre Pompidou x West Bund)
venues.note: David Chipperfield's opalescent-glass museum on the riverside, home to the landmark exhibition partnership with Paris's Centre Pompidou. Modern-art masterpieces from the Pompidou's collection, rotated in a serene daylit setting.

venues.name: Long Museum (West Bund)
venues.note: A dramatic concrete gallery of vaulted 'umbrella' arches, holding one of China's most important private collections from imperial art to the contemporary. The architecture alone rewards the visit; the shows are consistently ambitious.

venues.name: Yuz Museum
venues.note: A converted aircraft hangar on the West Bund turned into a soaring space for large-scale contemporary and immersive installations. The scale suits the blockbuster shows that draw Shanghai's art crowd.

venues.name: Power Station of Art
venues.note: China's first state-run contemporary art museum, set in a former power plant with its old chimney still marking the riverside. Home to the Shanghai Biennale and cavernous, industrial-scale installations.

venues.name: Wukang Road (Ferguson Lane area)
venues.note: The most photographed corner of the old French Concession, anchored by the ship-prow Wukang Mansion and lined with plane trees and 1920s villas. Stroll slowly with a coffee; the whole street is a period film set.

venues.name: Tianzifang
venues.note: A maze of shikumen lane houses reworked into tiny galleries, design boutiques, tea rooms and cafes. Tight and buzzing; a guide keeps the family together and points you to the makers worth stopping for.

venues.name: Xintiandi
venues.note: Restored stone-gate lane houses turned into an upscale district of restaurants, wine bars and flagship boutiques. The polished, safe, evening-out heart of old Shanghai, walkable and easy for multi-generation groups.

venues.name: The Plane-Tree Streets of the French Concession
venues.note: Wuyuan Road, Anfu Road, Fuxing Road and their neighbours form a leafy grid of villas, independent cafes and boutiques under a canopy of century-old planes. The most walkable, human-scaled Shanghai, best explored on foot with no fixed plan.

venues.name: Jing'an Temple
venues.note: A gilded Buddhist temple whose gold roofs sit startlingly against glass office towers on Nanjing West Road. Small but sumptuous, with a giant silver Buddha and a camphor-wood hall, an easy pause between shopping streets.

venues.name: Jade Buddha Temple
venues.note: An active monastery housing two Buddhas carved from single blocks of white Burmese jade, brought from Myanmar in the 1880s. Incense, chanting and a vegetarian temple kitchen make it a serene, veg-friendly stop.

venues.name: Nanjing Road (East & West)
venues.note: China's most famous shopping street, from the pedestrian neon stretch near the Bund to the luxury flagships of Nanjing West. A guide and driver let you cherry-pick the maisons and skip the crush.

venues.name: Shanghai Propaganda Poster Art Centre
venues.note: A private collection of thousands of Maoist-era and Cultural Revolution posters, now shown in a tower on Yan'an West Road after years hidden in a basement. Vivid, strange and unexpectedly moving; a guide gives the political context.

venues.name: M50 Art District (Moganshan Road)
venues.note: A cluster of galleries and studios in old textile-mill warehouses along Suzhou Creek, long the hub of Shanghai's contemporary scene. Graffiti-lined and gritty; go with a guide who knows which galleries are showing.

venues.name: Rockbund Art Museum
venues.note: A jewel-box contemporary museum in a restored 1932 Art Deco building a block behind the Bund. Tightly curated, ambitious shows in an intimate, beautifully restored setting.

venues.name: fu1015 / Historic Concession Villas
venues.note: The grand garden mansions of the old concession, some now private clubs, restaurants and galleries behind their walls. A curated visit inside one of these villas reveals the East-meets-West glamour of 1930s Shanghai.

venues.name: Rooftop Bars over the Bund
venues.note: Terraces such as Bar Rouge, the Peninsula's Sir Elly's and the towers of Pudong put the whole lit skyline at eye level with a cocktail in hand. The definitive Shanghai sundowner, reserved ahead for the best rail-side tables.

venues.name: Fuxing Park
venues.note: A formal French-style park where locals practise tai chi, dance and play chess under the trees each morning. A gentle, authentic slice of daily Shanghai life, lovely for grandparents and children between grander sights.

venues.name: People's Square & People's Park
venues.note: The green civic heart of the city, ringed by the Shanghai Museum, MoCA and the grand theatre, with the famous weekend 'marriage market' of parents' handwritten notices. A convenient, central anchor between museums.

venues.name: Suzhou Creek Waterfront Walk
venues.note: The revived creekside promenade lined with Art Deco warehouses, the historic post office and quiet cafes, far calmer than the Bund. A slow morning walk that shows the city's older, industrial romance.

venues.name: Shanghai Disneyland
venues.note: Asia's largest Disney park, with the world's biggest Enchanted Storybook Castle and its own distinctly Chinese touches. A full family day; a VIP tour guide skips the queues and choreographs the rides for a multi-gen group.

venues.name: Shanghai Ocean Aquarium
venues.note: A large modern aquarium beside the Oriental Pearl, with one of the longest underwater viewing tunnels in the world. A reliable crowd-pleaser for younger travellers within the Pudong sightseeing cluster.

venues.name: Tianzifang & Taikang Road Design Lanes
venues.note: The wider Taikang Road creative quarter around Tianzifang, dense with independent designers, ceramicists and studio-shops. Good for unhurried, one-of-a-kind gift-hunting away from the flagship stores.

venues.name: Longhua Temple & Pagoda
venues.note: Shanghai's largest and oldest temple complex, its leaning tenth-century pagoda rising beside working halls and a peach orchard that blooms in spring. Quieter than the central temples, with a vegetarian dining hall.

venues.name: Zhujiajiao Water Town
venues.note: The best-preserved of Shanghai's own canal towns, seventeen hundred years old, with stone arch bridges, willow-lined waterways and a hand-poled boat ride. Just over an hour by car, it makes an easy half-day escape into old Jiangnan.

venues.name: Qibao Old Town
venues.note: A compact canal town reachable on the metro, with a short old street of snack stalls, a small temple and a scattering of bridges. The closest water-town taste to the city centre when time is short.

venues.name: Zhouzhuang Water Town (Day Trip)
venues.note: The most famous of the ancient water towns, nine hundred years old, with fourteen stone bridges and preserved Ming and Qing dwellings mirrored in the canals. Go early with a private guide to have the bridges before the tour groups.

venues.name: Shanghai Grand Theatre / Symphony Hall
venues.note: World-class ballet, opera and orchestral programming in two architecturally striking halls, the acoustically superb Symphony Hall among them. A refined evening; the concierge secures the best boxes for touring companies.

venues.name: Bund Sightseeing & Waibaidu Bridge
venues.note: The steel Waibaidu Bridge and riverside gardens at the Bund's northern end frame the classic view where Suzhou Creek meets the Huangpu. A quiet, photogenic bookend to the main promenade.

venues.name: Bund Bull & Financial District Walk
venues.note: The Lujiazui skyway loops the three super-towers past the bronze Bund Bull and glass plazas, giving vertigo-free views up at the giants. An easy stroll that stitches the observation decks together.

venues.name: Shanghai History Museum (Shanghai Revolution Museum)
venues.note: Set in the former Shanghai Race Club building, it traces the city's rise from fishing village to global port with rich period detail. A well-told introduction that gives context to everything else you'll see.

venues.name: Cool Docks / South Bund Fabric & Antique Markets
venues.note: The South Bund fabric market lets you commission tailored qipao, suits and shirts in a day, near the riverside Cool Docks dining quarter. A practical, memorable stop for made-to-measure keepsakes of the trip.

venues.name: Speak Low
venues.note: Shingo Gokan's hidden multi-floor temple of drinks, enter through a sliding bookshelf and climb toward the serious pours.
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars, listed every year since 2016 (peak No. 10, 2017)

venues.name: Sober Company
venues.note: Shingo Gokan's all-day, all-night compound, café, izakaya and the Sober Society cocktail den built on Chinese ingredients.

venues.name: Epic
venues.note: A refined, spirit-forward bar with a Bund-side pedigree, precise classics and a long-standing place on the Asian list.

venues.name: Coa Shanghai
venues.note: The agave temple's Shanghai outpost, 200-plus tequilas and mezcals, and the hospitality that redefined the Asian bar.

venues.name: Pony Up
venues.note: An intimate, welcoming neighbourhood bar with real craft behind the counter, a fresh face on the Asian list.

venues.name: Union Trading Company
venues.note: Yao Lu's cornerstone of the modern Shanghai scene, the bar that defined what a great neighbourhood cocktail room could be.
credentials: Cornerstone of Shanghai's modern cocktail scene

venues.name: Flair Rooftop
venues.note: The Ritz-Carlton's 58th-floor terrace, the single most dramatic full-frontal view of the Bund with a drink in hand.
credentials: One of the city's highest rooftop bars

venues.name: Long Bar
venues.note: The restored 34-metre bar of the old Shanghai Club, where the city's tai-pans drank a century ago, poured with proper polish.
credentials: Waldorf Astoria Shanghai on the Bund (Forbes 4-Star hotel)
